en: The Blessed Lord said: I shall again declare that supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge.
Knowing which, all the sages have attained the supreme perfection from this world. //1//
Śrīdhara:

In the fourteenth [chapter], having refuted the independence of the spirit (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), he explains in detail the diversity of worldly existence resulting from attachment to the qualities (guṇas).
Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving,
know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field.
Thus it has been said.
And that conjunction of the field and the knower of the field is not independent, as it is for the atheistic Sāṅkhyas;
rather, it is preceded by the statement that it occurs through the will of the Lord. As for the cause, it is attachment to the qualities (guṇas) which leads to births in good and evil wombs.

Having stated this, and wishing to elaborate upon the manifold variety of saṃsāra characterized by the qualities of goodness (sattva) and the rest, the Blessed One praises the subject matter about to be described— which is of such a nature— with these two verses beginning with "Furthermore" (paraṃ bhūyaḥ). "Supreme" (param) means that which culminates in the Supreme Self (paramātman).
"Jñāna" (knowledge) is that by which something is known; it is instruction.
That knowledge I shall speak to you again with excellence.
Of what nature is it?

Among all forms of knowledge concerning austerity, ritual action, and so forth, this is the highest because it is the cause of liberation. He states this very point: "Having known which, all sages—those whose nature is contemplation—" [attain it].
From this bondage of the body, they have gone to— that is, attained— the supreme perfection, which is liberation. //1//
Madhusūdana:

In the preceding chapter, it was stated—“Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, know that to be from the union of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)” (Gītā 13.26). Therein, by thoroughly refuting the atheistic Sāṅkhya, the dependence of the union of the field and the knower of the field upon the Lord was established.
It must be explained:

thus it has been stated that "attachment to the qualities (guṇas) is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. In this regard, it must be explained: to which quality is there attachment, how does that attachment occur, what are the qualities, and how do they bind?

Likewise, it has been stated that "those who know the liberation from the material nature (bhūta-prakṛti) go to the Supreme. In this regard, it must be explained: how does liberation from the qualities designated as the material nature occur, and for one who is liberated—?
It must be stated what its characteristics are;
therefore, this fourteenth chapter is commenced to explain all of this in detail.
In that regard, praising the subject matter about to be explained with two verses in order to generate interest in the listeners, the Blessed Lord said: "The Supreme."
By this [means], knowledge is known— that is, the supreme means for attaining knowledge of the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is most excellent because it has the Supreme Reality as its object.
Of what nature is that?
Among the external means of knowledge, such as sacrifices and the like, this is the best because it yields the highest fruit;
however, humility and the other qualities are not [the best among those], since they are internal means and thus yield the highest fruit.
By the word "supreme" (param), its superior object is indicated.
The distinction is that by the word "supreme" (uttama), its state of having an exalted fruit is indicated.

I shall proclaim again—that is, once more—such knowledge, even though it has been stated repeatedly in previous chapters; for having known and practiced this knowledge, all the sages (munayaḥ)—those characterized by reflection, namely the renunciants (saṃnyāsinaḥ)—attained the supreme perfection called liberation (mokṣa).
Having departed from this bondage of the body, they have attained [liberation]. //1//
Viśvanātha:
The qualities (guṇas) are the binders; they are to be known by their fruits in the fourteenth [chapter].
When the qualities have ceased, the multitude of signs and devotion are described as the cause.
In the preceding chapter, it was stated: "Attachment to the qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs.
In that regard, what are the qualities, and of what nature is attachment to the qualities?
In response to the inquiry as to which fruit results from association with which quality,
what the characteristic of one endowed with the qualities is,
or how liberation from the qualities occurs, the author makes a promise to speak while praising the subject matter about to be explained by saying "The Supreme."
That by which something is known is "knowledge" (jñāna), namely the supreme and most excellent instruction (upadeśa). //1//
Baladeva said:
"The three qualities (guṇas) are indeed the bondages; they are to be understood through their fruits.
Their cessation occurs through devotion to Me—thus it was declared in the fourteenth [chapter]."

In the preceding chapter, having distinguished the essential natures of *prakṛti*, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*) as they exist in mutual association, it was stated that one who knows them and is distinguished by qualities such as humility is liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*; furthermore, attachment to the *guṇas* was declared to be the cause of that bondage.
In this regard, what are the *guṇas*?
In response to the inquiry—“In what quality is there attachment, and how? What is the fruit resulting from attachment to which quality?

What is the characteristic of one attached to the qualities, or how is liberation from the qualities attained?”—the Blessed One praises the Supreme with two verses in order to generate a personal inclination toward the subject about to be explained.

Furthermore, I shall speak again of another knowledge concerning the *guṇas*, which is distinct from what was previously mentioned and pertains specifically to *prakṛti* and the individual soul (*jīva*). This knowledge is the most excellent and supreme among all forms of knowledge regarding *prakṛti* and the *jīva*, because it has been extracted like butter.
Having known and realized this, all the sages—those whose nature is contemplation—have attained the supreme perfection in this world, characterized by the realization of the true nature of the Self.
Or, "knowledge" (jñāna) is that by which something is known, namely instruction;
and although that has been mentioned previously, I shall speak of it again in another manner.
And among the means of knowledge—such as austerity and the rest—it is the supreme, the most excellent, because it is an internal means for attaining that [knowledge].
Having known which, all the sages have attained from this world the supreme perfection characterized by liberation. //1//
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. 2.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having resorted to this": having resorted to this knowledge about to be described—that is, having performed these means of knowledge—and having attained my own nature (*sādharmya*), which is identity with me (*mad-rūpatva*), they are not born even during creation (*sarga*), when Brahmā and others are being produced.
Likewise, even at the time of dissolution they do not suffer;
they do not experience suffering during the dissolution.
The meaning is that they do not return [to worldly existence] again. //2//
Madhusūdana:
He shows the exclusivity of that [attainment] through the word "this" (*idam*).
Having resorted to—that is, having practiced—this aforementioned knowledge, which is the means to knowledge, one attains the state of similarity (*sādharmya*) with me, the Supreme Lord.
Having attained my own nature through absolute non-difference, they are not born even during creation when Hiraṇyagarbha and others are produced;
nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution, even when Brahmā perishes—the meaning being that they do not tremble, nor do they merge [into a state of unconsciousness]. //14.2//
Viśvanātha:
[They attain] liberation characterized by *sādharmya*, which is the state of having the same nature;
they do not suffer, nor do they experience distress. //2//
Baladeva says: "By this"—

meaning, by relying upon (upāśritya), that is, attaining, this knowledge which is about to be described through service to the Guru, all people, having attained similarity with Me, the Lord of All, whose eight qualities are eternally manifest, through those same eight qualities manifested by spiritual practice (*sādhana*), are not born again at the time of creation.

They do not become the objects of creation at the time of dissolution, nor do they suffer, nor do they undergo the state of being subject to death; thus, being free from birth and death, they become liberated.
Therefore, the plurality of individual souls (jīvas) is stated in relation to liberation.
This is understood from such scriptural passages as: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. //2//
My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings takes place. 3.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having directed the listener's attention through this praise, he now states the intended meaning—that nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), while subordinate to the Supreme Lord, are the causes for the origin of all beings, but not as independent entities—by saying "of Me" (mama).
It is called "great" (mahat) because it is unlimited by space and time.
It is called *brahma* because it has expanded its own effects, or because it is the cause of their growth;
the meaning is that it is *prakṛti*.
That great *brahma* is the womb—the place of conception—for me, the Supreme Lord.
In that [womb], I place—that is, I deposit—the seed, which is the manifestation of consciousness (cid-ābhāsa) and the cause for the expansion of the universe.

The meaning is this: at the time of creation, I unite with a "field" (kṣetra) suitable for experience the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who was dissolved in Me during the dissolution and possessed of the latent tendencies of ignorance, desire, and action.
From that implantation of the seed, the birth—meaning the origination—of all beings, beginning with Brahmā, occurs. //3//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, having first inclined the listener toward the subject through praise, [the author] now explains that while *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—which are dependent upon the Supreme Lord—are the causes for the production of all beings, they are not independent as is maintained in the Sāṅkhya doctrine. This...
He states the intended meaning with the two verses beginning "My womb" (*mama yoniḥ*).

It is called *mahat* (the Great) because it is superior in relation to all effects. It is called *brahman* because of its nourishing nature (*bṛṃhaṇatvāt*), consisting in being the cause of the growth of all effects.
The unmanifest is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is *māyā* or the Great Brahman.

That Great Brahman is my, the Lord’s, womb—the place of conception. Into that great womb, the Brahman, I place the seed, which is the cause of the birth of all beings, in the form of a resolve characterized by the vision: "May I become many; may I procreate."
"I maintain" means "I make that the object of my resolve.
For instance,

a certain father, desiring a son who will continue his lineage, conceives a fetus in the womb— preceded by the emission of semen— in order to unite with his own body that [son] which has merged into him in the form of food such as rice.
And from that moment of conception, that son becomes united with a body;
for that purpose, the intermediate stages such as the *kalala* and so forth occur.

Likewise, at the time of creation, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who was merged within Me during the dissolution and possessed of the latent tendencies of ignorance, desire, and action, [becomes joined] with the field of experience—a composite of causes and effects.

In order to effect this, O Bhārata, I first pour forth the seed known as the reflection of consciousness (cid-ābhāsa) and then conceive the embryo in the form of the activity of Māyā; for that purpose, [the creation of] Hiraṇyagarbha and the others occurs, but not without the conception of the embryo performed by the Lord—this is the meaning. //14.3//
Viśvanātha:

Now, in order to explain the manner in which attachment to the *guṇas*—produced by beginningless ignorance—is the cause of bondage, he describes the manner of the manifestation of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*): "The womb of Me, the Supreme Lord, the place for the depositing of the seed, is the Great Brahman."
Because it is not limited by space or time, it is "great" (mahat);
because it is the cause of expansion—that is, growth—in the form of its effects, it is Brahman, meaning it is the primordial nature (prakṛti).
Furthermore, in some scriptural passages, Brahman is indeed designated as the primordial nature.
"In that [nature], I place and deposit the embryo.

By the words "But know My other nature, higher than this, which consists of the individual soul (jīva)," that nature of the individual soul— which is a mass of consciousness and is indicated as being of the nature of the marginal power (taṭastha-śakti)— is here called by the term "embryo" in its capacity as the life-force of all living beings.
From that act of impregnation performed by me, there arises—the birth and manifestation—of all beings, beginning with Brahmā. //3//

Baladeva: Thus, having generated in the listener an inclination toward that very subject matter through its praise, [the author] now clarifies—in the verse beginning with "Whatever is born" (*yāvat sañjāyate kiñcit*)—the intended union of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), which is caused by the Supreme Lord (*pareśa*), in accordance with the meaning of the two preceding verses beginning with "Earth, water... (*bhūmir āpaḥ*). He does so by means of the word "mine" (*mama*).

The Great One, the cause of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), namely *pradhāna*—which possesses manifest qualities such as *sattva* and the rest—is the womb, the place of gestation, for me, the sovereign of all who create millions of cosmic eggs. Furthermore, the word "Brahman" is applied to *pradhāna*; therefore, this [world] called name, form, and food is born from it.
Thus says the Śruti.

In that great Brahman, which serves as the womb, I place—that is, I deposit—the embryo, which is a mass of atomic consciousness. That insentient Prakṛti which was described by the words "earth, water," and so forth, is here called "great Brahman."

The meaning is as follows: by the verse beginning with "itas tv anyām," that conscious nature (*cetanā prakṛti*) which was previously described is here referred to by the word "womb" (*garbha*), because it is the seed of all living beings. Thus, the sense is: "I unite the class of conscious enjoyers with the insentient nature (*prakṛti*) which serves as the field of experience. Then, from the union of these two natures—which has the Great Principle (*mahat*) as its cause—or from the "impregnation" (*garbhādhāna*), there arises the birth and manifestation of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. //3//
O son of Kuntī, whatever forms are produced in all wombs, their great womb is Brahman; I am the father who provides the seed. 14.4

Śrīdhara: This process of the origin of beings occurs not only at the commencement of creation through my superintendence of these two—prakṛti and puruṣa—but rather at all times. Thus he says "sarva" (all):

in all wombs, such as those of humans and so forth, whatever forms consisting of the stationary and the moving are produced, for those forms, the Great Brahman—that is, prakṛti—is the womb, standing in the place of a mother.
And I am the father who provides the seed; the father is the one who performs the impregnation. //4//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might object: "How can all beings arise from Him, since specific bodies such as those of gods and others originate from other causes? Anticipating this doubt, He says: "In all wombs" (*sarva-yoniṣu*).

O Kaunteya, in all wombs—whether they be gods, ancestors, humans, cattle, wild animals, and so forth—whatever forms arise, distinguished by various types such as those born from a womb, from an egg, or from sprouts, and possessing diverse structures and bodies; [all these arise from Me].

Of those forms, the Great Brahman itself—which has assumed the state of their respective causes—is the womb, standing in the place of the mother. I, the Supreme Lord, am the provider of the seed, the father who performs the act of impregnation.
Therefore, it is rightly said that "the origin of all beings proceeds from that," because the various specific states of the Great Brahman alone constitute the other causes. //4//
Viśvanātha:

It is not only at the time of the origin of creation that Prakṛti is the mother of all beings and I am the father; rather, it is so at all times. Thus he says: "In all wombs," from those of the gods down to the level of a blade of grass, whatever forms there are, consisting of both the moving and the stationary.
From those forms arises the Great Brahman, which is Nature (prakṛti)—the womb, the place of origin, and the mother;
and I am the provider of the seed, the father who performs the act of impregnation. //4//
Baladeva: "In all," etc.

O Kaunteya, among all wombs—from the gods down to the stationary beings—whatever forms or bodies come into existence, for those the Great Brahman, which is Pradhāna, is the womb; that is to say, it is the cause of their origin, their mother.
I am the Supreme Lord, the Father, who bestows life by joining the mass of atomic consciousnesses in accordance with their respective karmas. //4//
Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities born of material nature, O mighty-armed one, bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body. (14.5)

Śrīdhara: Thus, having described the origin of all beings from *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which are dependent upon the Supreme Lord, he now elaborates upon the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the *puruṣa* through its conjunction with *prakṛti* by means of fourteen verses beginning with "sattvam.
The three qualities (*guṇas*) known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* originate from *prakṛti*.
Those whose origin or emergence is from *prakṛti* are so described.
*Prakṛti* is the equilibrium of the *guṇas*.
Having become manifested through separation from that [equilibrium], they abide in identity with the body, which is the effect of *prakṛti*.

The meaning is that they bind the embodied soul—which is in reality an imperishable and changeless portion of consciousness—by means of their own effects, namely pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth; that is, they yoke it to them. //5//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, by refuting the atheistic Sāṅkhya, it has been stated that the conjunction of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is dependent upon the Lord (Īśvara). Now, in which quality (guṇa) does attachment reside?
What are these qualities (guṇas),
and how do they bind?
This is explained by the fourteen verses beginning with "sattvam" and ending before "anyam."
The qualities (guṇas) named sattva, rajas, and tamas are eternally dependent upon the Puruṣa, because all insentient things exist for the sake of the sentient.
However, unlike color and other attributes in the Vaiśeṣika system, they do not reside as substrates within a substance.
Furthermore, no distinction between quality and the possessor of quality is intended here, because primordial matter (prakṛti) consists of the three qualities themselves.
If so, how can they be said to arise from *prakṛti*?

It is explained as follows: *Prakṛti*, also called *māyā*, is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*. From that [state], when they undergo transformation into a state of disequilibrium through the relationship of mutual dominance and subordination (*aṅgāṅgi-bhāva*), they are said to arise from *prakṛti*.

And these [afflictions] bind the embodied soul— the individual self (*jīva*) who, through the superimposition of identity with the body, has fallen into the state of being a "possessor of a body" within this aggregate of the physical body and senses, which is the product of *prakṛti*—
binding that which is in reality immutable because it is devoid of all modifications. Though the self is truly changeless,

they make it appear as if possessed of their own modifications through delusion, just as vessels of water, by means of the superimposition of reflections, make the sun situated in the sky appear to possess their own changes.
Because it possesses its own vibration and so forth.
And how there is no ultimate bondage has been explained previously: "Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, it neither acts nor is tainted" (Gītā 13.32). //5//
Viśvanātha:
Having thus described the origin of all beings from Prakṛti and Puruṣa, he now speaks of the *guṇas*.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of bondage the individual soul (*jīva*) undergoes through attachment to them, he says: "Sattva... and so forth.

The qualities bind the embodied soul—the individual living being who, though in reality imperishable, changeless, and unattached, exists through a sense of identity with the body which is a product of material nature—solely due to attachment to the qualities caused by beginningless ignorance. //5//
Baladeva: Now, as to what the qualities are, how the person becomes attached to them, and how they bind him, he says in four verses beginning with "sattva":

There are three qualities known as *sattva* and so forth, which originate from *prakṛti*, being manifested from *prakṛti*. These bind the person—who, though situated in the body which is their own effect, is imperishable and in reality changeless—to themselves by means of [objects] grasped through non-discrimination.
They join him with their own natures—pleasure, pain, and delusion. //5//
Therein, O sinless one, *sattva*, because of its purity, is illuminating and free from affliction; it binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge. (14.6)
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he explains the manner in which *sattva* acts as a binder with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Among those qualities (*guṇas*), *sattva*, because of its stainlessness and clarity, is illuminating and radiant like a crystal gem; it is also "healthy," meaning free from affliction, and "peaceful. This is the meaning.
Therefore, because of its quality of tranquility, it binds by means of attachment to its own effect, which is pleasure;
and because of its quality of illumination, it also binds by means of attachment to its own effect, which is knowledge.
O sinless one, free from fault!
The meaning is that it joins the mental attributes—such as "I am happy" and "I am wise"—to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who identifies with them. //6//
Madhusūdana: Regarding that,
it is said "therein" (tatra) to explain what quality binds by means of what attachment.
Among those qualities (*guṇas*), *sattva* is illuminating; it removes the concealment caused by the quality of *tamas* regarding consciousness (*caitanya*).
This is because, due to its stainlessness and clarity, it is—so to speak—capable of receiving the reflection of consciousness.
Not only does it manifest consciousness, but it is also free from affliction (*anāmaya*).

The meaning is that disease is suffering, and its opposite is that which manifests pleasure; it binds the embodied being through attachment to pleasure. O sinless one, O you who are free from addiction!
In all instances, the intention behind the vocatives has been stated previously and should be kept in mind.
Here, by the words "pleasure" (*sukha*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-pariṇāma*) which manifest them are meant;

for both pleasure and consciousness are listed as attributes of the field (*kṣetra-dharma*) alongside desire and the rest, in the passage: "Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude" (Gītā 13.7).
In that regard, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self of pleasure and knowledge, which are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), takes the form "I am attached" and "I know.
For an attribute of an object cannot belong to the subject.
Therefore, this is merely ignorance (*avidyā-mātra*); as has been stated hundreds of times previously. //6//
Viśvanātha:
Regarding that, he states the definition of *sattva* and the manner in which it acts as a binder with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
"Free from affliction" (*anāmaya*) means being without calamity, that is, peaceful (*śānta*).

Because it is peaceful, there is an attachment to its own effect, which is pleasure; and because it is illuminating, there is an attachment to its own effect, which is knowledge. Through ignorance alone, the individual soul (jīva) identifies with these two attributes of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), thinking "I am happy" and "I am wise.
It is by means of this that [the intellect] binds him.
O sinless one, the sense is: do not appropriate the sin characterized by the false identification (abhimāna) that "I am happy" and "I am wise. //6//
Baladeva: Now, with three verses beginning with "tatra," he states the characteristics of the three qualities—sattva and the others—and the modes in which they act as bondages.
Among those three, *prakāśaka* means that which manifests knowledge; *anāmaya* means free from disease, meaning it manifests happiness which is the opposite of suffering.
Why is this so?
Because of its stainlessness and clarity,
*sattva* is likewise the cause of illumination and happiness.

And that *sattva* binds the *puruṣa* through the conjunction with its own effects— namely, knowledge and happiness— which consists of the egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*) "I am the knower" and "I am happy."
This knowledge should be understood as having for its object the true nature of worldly things, and this happiness as consisting in the clarity of the body and the senses.
When there is attachment to various objects, there is engagement in actions which are the means to them; from those actions arises birth in bodies which are the means to experience their fruits.
And again, because there is attachment to those [bodies], there is no liberation from *sattva*. //6//
Know that *rajas* consists of passion and arises from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action. (14.7)
Śrīdhara: He states the characteristic and the binding nature of *rajas* in the verse beginning with "Rajas.
Know that the quality known as *rajas* is of the nature of passion (*rāga*), consisting of attachment (*anurañjana*).
For this very reason, it arises from thirst and clinging (*tṛṣṇāsaṅga*).
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the longing for an object not yet attained;
attachment (*saṅga*) is the delight in an object already attained, a specific form of clinging.

Since that passion (*rajas*) is the source from which both craving and attachment arise, it binds the embodied being intensely through attachment—that is, clinging—to actions concerning objects both seen and unseen.
The meaning is that, indeed, through craving and attachment, there arises an adherence to karmas. //7//
Madhusūdana:

*Rāga* is that by which a person becomes attached (*rajyate*) to sense objects; it is desire (*kāma*), greed (*gardha*). Know that *rajas* has that very [desire] as its essence (*ātmā*), its own nature, because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). For this very reason, it is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), the longing for what has not yet been attained.

Attachment (*āsakti*) is the desire to preserve that which has been acquired even when its destruction is imminent; since that passion (*rajas*) gives rise to both thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) and attachment (*āsakti*), O Kaunteya, it binds one through attachment to action (*karma-saṅga*)—that is, in actions for the sake of seen or unseen results, with the thought: "I am doing this; I shall enjoy this fruit."
Due to a particular form of attachment, the embodied being—who in reality is a non-agent—is one who possesses the conceit of agency, because rajas is the cause of active engagement. //7//
Viśvanātha:
Know that the quality of *rajas* consists of passion (*rāga*), which is of the nature of attachment;
*tṛṣṇā* is the longing for an object not yet attained.
Attachment (*saṅga*) is clinging to an object already attained.

That from which the emergence of these two [passion and delusion] arises is *rajas*. It binds the embodied being through attachment—that is, clinging—to actions for the sake of seen and unseen objects; through thirst and attachment, there arises an addiction to actions. (7)

Baladeva: *Rajas* means passion (*rāga*), which is the mutual desire between man and woman; it is so called because of the identity between that [passion] and its effects, which cause the increase of *rajas*.
And that [state] arises from thirst and the like: *tṛṣṇā* is the longing for objects such as sound;
*saṅga* is the attachment to the company of sons, friends, and so forth; [the word refers to that] from which the origin of those two arises.
And thus, passion (*rajas*) is the cause of attachment through craving and lust.
That *rajas* binds the embodied person (*dehin*) through attachment—that is, through longing—for actions that result in the attainment of women, objects of sense, sons, and so forth.
Through a desire for women and the like, one performs actions.
These [passions] lead one to women and other objects that serve as the means for experiencing those fruits;
thus, because it occurs again and again in this way, there is no liberation from rajas. //7//
But know that *tamas* arises from ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep. (14.8)
Śrīdhara: He states the characteristic of *tamas* and its binding nature with the word "tamas.
The meaning is: know that *tamas* arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*), having emerged from a portion of *prakṛti* in which the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) predominates;
therefore, it deludes all embodied beings, generating confusion.
Therefore, that *tamas* binds the embodied being through negligence, laziness, and sleep. In this context, negligence is a lack of attentiveness; laziness is a lack of exertion.
Drowsiness is the sinking of the mind due to depression. //8//
Madhusūdana:
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of highlighting the distinction [of tamas] with respect to sattva and rajas.
Know that tamas is born of ignorance—that which has arisen from ignorance in the form of the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*).
Therefore, for all embodied beings, this delusion— which consists of non-discrimination and generates error—
is bound by negligence, laziness, and sleep;
the term "embodied being" is understood to carry over from the previous context.

O Bhārata, negligence (pramāda) is the incapacity to discern objects; it is opposed to illumination, which is the function of sattva. Laziness (ālasya) is the incapacity for activity; it is opposed to engagement, which is the function of rajas.
Sleep is the mental modification that is opposed to both [illumination and activity] and has the quality of darkness (tamas) as its objective support; this is the distinction. //8//
Viśvanātha:

"Born of ignorance" (*ajñānaja*) means that [delusion] is perceived or inferred as having arisen from its own fruit, which is ignorance; thus, it means that which generates ignorance. "Delusive" (*mohana*) means that which generates error.
Heedlessness is lack of attention; laziness is a lack of exertion;
sleep is the sinking of the mind due to its depression. //8//
Baladeva: "But it is *tamas*.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from the second [category] mentioned previously.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the comprehension of the true nature of reality; ignorance (*ajñāna*) is that portion of *prakṛti* which primarily possesses the quality of veiling that which is opposed to such knowledge.
From that [rajas] is born tamas, which deludes all embodied beings and generates erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*).
Thus, tamas is that which obscures the knowledge of the true nature of reality and produces erroneous cognition;
that tamas binds the person (*puruṣa*) through its own effects, such as negligence (*pramāda*) and the like.

In this context, negligence (*pramāda*) is a lack of attention, consisting in engagement in improper action, and it is opposed to the illumination that is the function of *sattva*. Laziness (*ālasya*) is a lack of exertion,
and it is opposed to the activity that is the function of *rajas*.
But sleep, which is opposed to both of those, consists in the depression of the mind. //8//
Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bharata, and rajas to action;
but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence. (14.9)
Śrīdhara: He states the excellence of the capacity of *sattva* and the other qualities in performing their respective functions with the words "Sattva...
*Sattva* attaches—that is, it causes union—with happiness;
the meaning is that even when there is a cause for pain, grief, and so forth, it makes the embodied being face toward happiness alone.
Thus, even when the cause of pleasure and so forth is present, *rajas* attaches one specifically to action;
whereas *tamas*, although knowledge is being produced through association with the Great Principle (*mahat*), veils and obscures that knowledge, attaching one to negligence—
that is, it joins one to a lack of attention toward the meaning taught by the great ones.
The meaning is that it also joins [the mind] with such states as laziness. //9//
Madhusūdana:
Viśvanātha:
He demonstrates once again, in brief, the very meaning already stated.
The meaning is that *sattva*, acting as the agent, attaches—that is, brings under its control and binds—the individual soul (*jīva*) which is attached to its own fruit of pleasure.
*Rajas*, acting as the agent, binds the individual soul which is attached to actions.
*Tamas*, acting as the agent, having veiled knowledge and produced ignorance, binds that [soul] which is intent upon negligence. //9//
Baladeva: He states in two verses beginning with "sattvam" that the qualities, being non-dual and preeminent, expand into their respective effects.
Sattva, when predominant, attaches the person to its own effect, which is pleasure;
rajas, when predominant, attaches him to actions.
That supreme darkness, existing in negligence, binds him; the meaning is that it does so by veiling knowledge and producing ignorance. //9//
Overpowering both passion and darkness, goodness prevails, O Bhārata; likewise, passion overcomes goodness and darkness, and darkness overcomes goodness and passion. (14.10)
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this: "Rajas... and so forth. Sattva comes into being by overcoming—that is, eclipsing—the two qualities of rajas and tamas;
it arises through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
The meaning is that it then becomes attached to its own effects, such as pleasure, knowledge, and so forth.
In the same way, rajas also arises by overpowering the two qualities, sattva and tamas;
it then becomes attached to its own effects, such as craving, action, and so forth.
In this way, tamas also arises by overpowering both the qualities of sattva and rajas;
consequently, it attaches one to its own effects, such as negligence and laziness—this is the meaning. //10//
Madhusūdana: It was asked, "When do the qualities perform their functions? To this it is replied: "Rajas... [and so forth].

When *sattva* prevails, arising and increasing while simultaneously overcoming both *rajas* and *tamas*, then it performs its own specific effect, as previously described; this is the implied meaning.
Likewise, when *rajas* prevails, arising while overcoming the two qualities *sattva* and *tamas*, [it performs its own specific effect].
Then it performs its own function as previously described.
Likewise, when tamas also arises having overwhelmed both the qualities of sattva and rajas, then it performs its own function as previously described; this is the meaning. //10//
Viśvanātha:

Having stated that the qualities (*guṇas*) prevail toward their respective effects such as pleasure and so forth, he says—in response to the inquiry as to how they do so—that *sattva* comes into being by overcoming, that is, eclipsing, the other two qualities, *rajas* and *tamas*;
it arises through the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

In this way, rajas also arises by overpowering both sattva and tamas through the power of such unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); likewise, tamas also arises by overpowering both the qualities of sattva and rajas. //10//

Baladeva: If it is asked how one among three equal [qualities] can suddenly attain preeminence, you have stated that this occurs through the arising of such past karma and through such food; thus, "rajas" [is mentioned].
Sattva, as the agent, becomes preeminent by overcoming—that is, eclipsing—rajas and tamas. Rajas, as the agent, becomes preeminent by overcoming sattva and tamas.
Tamas becomes predominant by overpowering both sattva and rajas;
when it is predominant, the implication is that it performs its own specific, previously mentioned function. //10//
When illumination arises through all the gates in this body, one should then know that goodness (sattva) has increased. 14.11
Śrīdhara: Now, with the three verses beginning "In all the gates," he states the signs of the increased states of *sattva* and the others.

When, in this body which is the abode of the self's experience, a light consisting of the cognition of sound and other objects arises—that is, is produced—in all the gates such as the ears and so forth, then by this sign of light one should know (*vidyāt*), that is, recognize, that *sattva* has increased.
Furthermore, it has been stated that one may also know [the object] through the word "uta" and by means of signs such as pleasure. //11//
Madhusūdana:
Now, with the verse beginning "In all the gates" (13.16), he describes the signs of those [states] that have arisen.

In this body, which is the abode of the self's experience, when light—in the form of a specific modification of the intellect (*buddhi*) taking on the shape of an object and opposed to the obscuration of its own object—arises in all the gates, that is, in all the instruments such as the ears and so forth, which are the means of perception; [then...]

That very same cognition arises with respect to objects such as sound; then, by this mark (liṅga) known as the cognition of objects such as sound, one should know—that is, one should understand—that the luminous *sattva* has increased and become manifest.
The meaning is that one may also know it by means of marks such as pleasure and so forth. //11//
Viśvanātha:
It has been stated that Vardhamāna is indeed a quality (guṇa) which, by its own nature, causes the other two qualities to appear diminished relative to itself.
Therefore, he describes the signs of their increase with the following three verses beginning with "sarva-".
When there is illumination through all the doors, such as the ears and so forth—
of what nature?
When knowledge consisting of the correct cognition of Vedic words and the like arises, then one should know that the quality of *sattva* has increased by that very sign of such knowledge.
Because of the word "ut," it is that which reaches forth the light whose nature is the bliss arising from the Self. //11//
Baladeva: With three verses beginning with "sarva," he describes the signs of the predominance of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*.

When knowledge arises through all the gates of perception—the ears and so forth—in the form of the illumination of the true nature of sound and the rest, then, by the sign of such knowledge, one should know that *sattva* has increased in this body.
The word "uta" is used in the sense of "also";
the meaning is that one should know that [the Self] even by means of the mark of pleasure. //11//
Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing— these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas. (14.12)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, as for "greed" (lobha):
greed is the desire that increases again and again even when there is the acquisition of wealth and other such things. "Activity" (pravṛtti) is the state of constantly acting.
The undertaking of actions is the exertion in constructing large houses and the like.
Restlessness is the non-cessation of conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts, such as "Having done this, I shall do that.
Longing is the desire to seize various objects, high or low, as soon as they are seen, here and there.
When rajas has increased, these signs arise;
the meaning is that by these one should recognize the increase of tamas. //12//
Madhusūdana:

Greed (*lobha*) is that particular desire which increases moment by moment even when a great acquisition of wealth is occurring, and which cannot be turned back until its object is attained; in other words, it is a specific form of longing. Activity (*pravṛtti*) is the state of being constantly and diligently striving.
*Ārambha* is the undertaking of activities involving great expenditure of wealth and effort, directed toward objects such as optional rites, forbidden acts, or worldly matters like large houses;
*aśama* is the non-cessation of the flow of volitions, thinking "having done this, I shall do that";
and *spṛhā* is the desire to acquire by any means whatsoever the various riches of others as soon as they are seen.
When *rajas*, which is of the nature of passion, has increased, these signs characterized by passion arise.
O bull among the Bharatas!
The meaning is that one should recognize that *rajas* has increased by these signs. //12//
Viśvanātha:

*Pravṛtti* is the state of being intent on various efforts; it is the undertaking of actions, such as the exertion involved in building houses and the like. *Aśama* is the non-cessation of the enjoyment of sense objects. //12//
Baladeva: Greed is the state of being intent on not relinquishing one's own wealth.
Activity is the state of being intent on efforts to increase that [wealth].
The undertaking of actions refers to the commencement of activities such as house-building and the like.
Lack of tranquility is the failure of the senses to cease from the enjoyment of sense-objects;
longing is the desire for sense-objects.
By these signs, one should know that rajas has increased. //12//
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion— these arise when Tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus. (14.13)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the term "aprakāśa":
*aprakāśa* means the loss of discrimination;
*apravṛtti* means a lack of effort.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is the absence of reflection upon what ought to be done;
delusion (*moha*) is false attachment.
When darkness (*tamas*) has increased, these signs arise.
The meaning is that one should understand the increase of *tamas* by these [signs]. //13//
Madhusūdana:

"Lack of illumination" (*aprakāśa*) means the total incapacity for comprehension despite the presence of causes of understanding such as instruction and the like; and "lack of engagement" (*apravṛtti*) means the total incapacity for engagement with the scripture despite the presence of causes for engagement—such as the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—and even when understanding has been produced.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is the absence of reflection upon an object that has presented itself as something to be done at that time.
Delusion (*moha*) itself is delusion; it is either sleep or error.
The particle *ca* is used for conjunction.
The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
O descendant of Kuru, these symptoms arise only when darkness has increased;
therefore, the meaning is that one should recognize increased darkness by means of these non-deviating symptoms. //13//
Viśvanātha:
Non-manifestation is the absence of discrimination;
it is the apprehension of sound and other objects not prescribed by the scriptures.
Non-engagement (*apravṛtti*) is the mere absence of effort.
Negligence (*pramāda*) is the conviction that "it does not exist" even when an object is held in the throat or elsewhere.
Delusion (*moha*) is false attachment. //13//

Baladeva: Non-illumination (*aprakāśa*) is the absence of knowledge. Non-engagement (*apravṛtti*) is the grasping of objects not prescribed by the scriptures, consisting in an aversion to action. Negligence (*pramāda*) is the conviction that an object does not exist even when it is in one's hand or elsewhere; delusion (*moha*) is false attachment.
One should recognize that darkness has increased by these signs. //13//
But when the embodied soul meets its end while goodness (sattva) is predominant, then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest. 14.14
Śrīdhara: With the two verses beginning with "yadā," he describes the specific results of the qualities such as *sattva* when they have increased at the very time of death.

When the individual soul (*jīva*) meets death while *sattva* has increased, then there are those who know and worship the highest [beings] such as Hiraṇyagarbha; these are the "knowers of the highest" (*uttama-vidaḥ*). Their worlds are stainless and consist of light—specific locations for the enjoyment of happiness.
He practices them and attains them. //14//
Madhusūdana:
Now, with two verses beginning with "yadā," He describes the specific results of the qualities such as *sattva* when they have increased at the time of death.
When *sattva* has increased, if the embodied one—the living being who identifies with the body—meets his end or reaches dissolution (*pralaya*), [he attains a particular state].

Then, he attains—that is, reaches—the stainless worlds of those who know that [Brahman], namely Hiraṇyagarbha and others; these are specific abodes for the enjoyment of divine pleasures, free from the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*. //14//
Viśvanātha:
"He goes to dissolution" means he meets death.
Then, those who find or obtain the highest [state] are the "knowers of the highest"—the worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha and others; [he grants them] their stainless worlds which bestow happiness. //14//
Baladeva: With the two verses beginning with "yadā," he describes the specific fruits of the qualities that have increased at the time of death.

When the embodied soul, the living being, meets its dissolution—that is, dies—at a time when *sattva* has increased, it attains and reaches the worlds of those who know the Supreme (*uttama-vidām*), such as the worshippers of Hiraṇyagarbha, which are endowed with divine enjoyments.
Pure, meaning free from the impurities of passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas). //14//
Having met its dissolution in rajas, it is born among those attached to action; likewise, dissolved in tamas, it is born in the wombs of the deluded. (14.15)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in passion" (rajasī):
when passion has increased, having met death, one is born among human beings who are attached to action.
Likewise, when darkness (tamas) has increased, being dissolved—that is, dead—one is born among the wombs of the deluded. //15//
Madhusūdana:

When rajas has increased, having undergone dissolution—that is, death—one is born among those attached to action, namely among human beings who are entitled to the fruits of actions prescribed or prohibited by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
Likewise, when tamas has increased, one who has dissolved—meaning one who has died—is born in the wombs of the deluded, such as among animals and the like. (15)
Viśvanātha:
Among those attached to action—that is, among men whose minds are clinging to ritual acts. //15//
Baladeva: When rajas has increased, a person, having met with dissolution—meaning death—is born among men who are attached to action, that is, those addicted to desire-driven rituals.
Likewise, when tamas has increased, a person who has dissolved—meaning died—is born in the wombs of the deluded, such as among animals and so forth. (15)
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by goodness (sattva);
the fruit of passion (rajas) is suffering, and the fruit of darkness (tamas) is ignorance. 14.16.
Śrīdhara: Now, he explains how sattva and the other qualities serve as causes for various fruits by means of their corresponding actions, beginning with the words "of action" (karmaṇaḥ).

They—the teachers such as Kapila and others—declare that the fruit of well-performed action, which is sāttvika action, is sāttvika: characterized primarily by sattva, stainless, and abounding in light, namely happiness.
"Of rajas" (rajasaḥ) means of rājasa action.
Since the discussion of the fruits of action is the subject at hand,
they say that its fruit is suffering;
"of darkness" (tamasaḥ) means of tamasic action.
They say that ignorance is its fruit, which is delusion;
and he will explain in the eighteenth chapter, with the words "the characteristics of sattvic and other actions are fixed, free from attachment," and so forth. //16//
Madhusūdana:
Now, by way of actions corresponding to their own nature, [the Lord] briefly states the variety of fruits resulting from *sattva* and the other *guṇas* with the words "of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*).

They say that the fruit of well-performed action—that is, action characterized by *sattva*, namely *dharma*—is *sāttvika*: produced by *sattva*, stainless, unmixed with the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, and happiness; so say the supreme sages.

But the fruit of *rājasa* action—that is, action characterized by passion which is mixed with sin and merit—is *rājasa* suffering: it abounds in pain and contains little pleasure, because the effect corresponds to its cause. Ignorance, consisting primarily of a lack of discrimination, is *tāmasa* suffering; it is the fruit of *tāmasa* action, that is, of unrighteousness (*adharma*).
The word "they say" is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].
And He will explain the characteristics of actions characterized by *sattva* and so forth in the eighteenth chapter, beginning with the words "obligatory, free from attachment," and so on.

Here, the words *rajas* and *tamas* are used for their effects, based on the metaphorical identification of cause and effect; just as in the mantra "melt the fat with cows" (*gobhiḥ śrīṇīta matsaram*), the word "cows" refers to the milk produced from them, or as in "you are grain, satisfy the gods" (*dhānyam asi dhinuhi devān*), the word "grain" [refers to the flour].
In that case, it refers to the rice produced from that [milk];
for here too, as in the case of milk and rice, the object (karman) is the subject under discussion. //16//
Viśvanātha:
Of good action—that is, of action characterized by *sattva*—the result is likewise *sāttvika*, pure and free from affliction.
Ignorance is insentience. //16//
Baladeva: Now, [the Lord] states that the qualities (*guṇas*) are the cause of diverse fruits by means of actions corresponding to themselves, beginning with the words "Of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*).

Sages who know the nature of the qualities say that the fruit of well-performed (*sukṛta*), i.e., *sāttvika* action, is stainless (*nirmala*). This means it is happiness (*sukha*) free from the characteristics of the fruits of *rajas* and *tamas*, which consist of impurity, suffering, and delusion.
And that [happiness] is *sāttvika*, produced by *sattva*.

The fruit of *rājasa* action—that is, action characterized by *rajas*—is suffering; because the effect conforms to its cause, the meaning is that it consists mostly of suffering with only a trace of pleasure.
For the fruit of *tāmasa* action—that is, action characterized by *tamas*, such as violence—is suffering consisting primarily of a consciousness of ignorance; this is the meaning.

In this context, by the words *rajas* and *tamas*, the actions characterized as *rājasa* and *tāmasa* are indicated, just as in the phrase "satiated with the cows' [milk]," the word *go* indicates cow's milk.
The characteristics of *sāttvika* and other types of action will be described in the eighteenth chapter through such phrases as "constant and free from attachment. (16)
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas*, greed; from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself. (14.17)

Śrīdhara: He states the reason for that very point in the words "from goodness" (sattvāt). From goodness, knowledge arises; therefore, the fruit of action characterized by goodness is happiness abounding in illumination.
From *rajas* arises greed;
and because that is a cause of suffering, action preceded by it results in suffering as its fruit.
From *tamas*, however, arise negligence, delusion, and ignorance.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is entirely logical that the fruit of tamasic action is the attainment of ignorance. //17//
Madhusūdana:
Regarding this variety of fruits, he states the very reason previously mentioned, beginning with "from sattva.
Knowledge, which is of the nature of illumination and functions through all the instruments [of perception], arises from sattva.
Therefore, as a result corresponding to that, the fruit of sattvic action is happiness characterized by an abundance of illumination.
From rajas arises a specific longing—a greed for objects that cannot be stilled even by attaining the furthest reaches of sensory experience.
Because this longing, which constantly accumulates and can never be fulfilled, is always a cause of suffering, the fruit of the rājasic action preceded by it is suffering.
In this way, negligence and delusion arise from darkness (tamas),
and ignorance alone also arises.
The particle "eva" is intended to exclude illumination (prakāśa) and activity (pravṛtti).

Therefore, the meaning is that it is entirely logical that the fruit of tamasic action consists primarily of tamasic results such as ignorance and the like; and here, "ignorance" (ajñāna) means lack of light, while "negligence" (pramāda) and "delusion" (moha) have been explained in the passage beginning with "lack of light, non-activity... (Gītā 14.8). //17//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Regarding this variety of fruits, he states the very reason already mentioned: "from *sattva*.
From *sattva*, knowledge characterized by illumination arises.
Therefore, the fruit of *sāttvika* action is happiness abundant with illumination.

As for *rajas*, it is greed— a particular kind of thirst that is difficult to satiate even by indulging in millions of sense objects— and because this is a cause of suffering, the fruit of the action preceded by it is something abundant in suffering with a modicum of happiness.
From *tamas*, however, negligence and other such qualities arise; therefore, the fruit of action preceded by that is indeed suffering, characterized by an abundance of insentience. //17//

Those established in goodness (sattva) go upward; those characterized by passion (rajas) remain in the middle; and those of darkness (tamas), abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward. //18//
Śrīdhara: Now he describes the distinction of the fruits for those whose character consists of the functions of *sattva* and so forth, beginning with the word "upwards.
Those established in *sattva* (*sattvasthāḥ*) are those for whom the function of *sattva* is predominant.

They go upwards; the meaning is that, according to the gradations of the excellence of *sattva*, they attain the worlds—beginning with humans, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, and Devas, and reaching up to Satyaloka—which possess increasingly superior qualities and bliss.
Those characterized by passion (rājasas), however, being agitated by thirst and other such afflictions, remain in the middle;
they are born only in the world of humans.
The quality of darkness (tamas) is the lowest and most base.
Its function consists of negligence, delusion, and so forth. Those situated therein descend;
due to the varying degrees of the function of darkness (tamas), they are born in the hells such as Tāmisra and others. //18//
Madhusūdana:

Now, he describes by means of the terms "upward," "middle," and "downward" the very same results previously mentioned for those situated in the functions of *sattva* and the other qualities, according to their upward, middle, and downward states.
Here, because the word *vṛtta* (function) is joined with the third quality (*tamas*), it is intended that the term *vṛtta* applies to the first two qualities as well.

Those established in *sattva*, devoted to the conduct of *sattva* and to scriptural knowledge and action, go upwards as far as the world of *satyaloka* and are born among the gods; they do so according to the degree of their knowledge and action.

Likewise, those established in the middle, in the human world which is a mixture of merit and demerit, neither go upwards nor downwards, but are born among humans; these are the *rājasa* ones, devoted to actions characterized by the quality of *rajas* and preceded by greed and other such traits.

Those who abide in the activity of the lowest quality (jaghanya-guṇa-vṛttasthāḥ)— that is, those established in the activity of *tamas*, the lowest quality which follows after and is inferior to the other two qualities, such as sleep and laziness— go downward and are born among the lower classes. Since those abiding in the activity of the lowest quality may sometimes be *sāttvika* or *rājasa*, he says "those characterized by *tamas* (tāmasāḥ)," meaning those for whom *tamas* is always predominant.
The point is that for others, even if they occasionally abide in such conduct, it is not their primary characteristic. //18//
Viśvanātha:
Those established in *sattva* ascend, according to the degree of their *sattva*, as far as the world of truth (*satyaloka*);
those in the middle remain only in the world of humans (*manuṣyaloka*).
It is both "lowest" (jaghanya) and a "quality" (guṇa); its manifestation consists of negligence, indolence, and so forth. Those who abide therein go downward; they go to hell. //18//

Baladeva: Now, he describes those very fruits for those established in the functions of *sattva* and the other qualities, according to their being higher, middle, or lower, with the words "upwards" (*ūrdhvam*).
By the word "function" (*vṛtti*) in the context of *tamas*, the functions of the other two [qualities] are also intended.
Those established in *sattva*—meaning those fixed in the function of *sattva*—go upwards, as far as Satyaloka, in accordance with the degrees of *sattva*.
Those characterized by *rajas*—who are devoted to the functioning of *rajas*—abide in the middle world of humans, which is a mixture of merit and demerit;
they become human beings according to the varying degrees of their *rajas*.

However, those who abide in the functioning of the lowest quality, known as *tamas*, which is inferior in comparison to *sattva* and *rajas*, go downward due to negligence and other such traits; according to the varying degrees of their *tamas*, they enter the wombs of animals, birds, immobile beings, and so forth.
The statement that they "are called tāmasas" reveals their perpetual abiding in darkness. //18//
When one perceives no agent other than the qualities,
and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state of being. (14.19)

Śrīdhara: Thus, having described the manifold expansion of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) caused by attachment to the qualities of *prakṛti*, he now shows liberation through discernment of that [expansion] with the words "not another" (*nānyam*).

When, however, the seer becomes discriminative and does not perceive any agent other than the qualities—which have transformed into the forms of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—but rather perceives that "the qualities alone perform actions," [then he attains liberation].
And he knows the Self, which is beyond and distinct from the qualities, as their witness;
he indeed attains, that is, reaches, my state, which is Brahmanhood. //19//
Madhusūdana:
In this chapter, three subjects were introduced as being about to be explained.

Among them, two points have been stated: that the conjunction of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is dependent upon the Lord, and what the qualities (guṇas) are and how they bind.
Now, however, it remains to be stated how liberation from the *guṇas* occurs and what the characteristic of the liberated one is.
In this regard, he says "not another" (*nānyam*) to show that because the *guṇas* consist of false knowledge, liberation from them comes through right knowledge.
When the seer, skilled in inquiry, perceives another—the agent—as distinct from the *guṇas*, which have transformed into the forms of effects, causes, and objects; [then liberation occurs].

He perceives the "sat" (Being) and does not perceive the "vicāra" (discursive thought). He sees that it is the *guṇas* themselves—having assumed the states of the internal organ, the external organs, the body, and their objects—that are the agents of all actions.

And he perceives that which is beyond the *guṇas* as they transform through their various specific conditions; [he perceives] that which is untouched by the *guṇas* and their effects, and which illumines them, just as the sun is untouched by the water or its ripples.
He who knows the one Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is changeless, the witness of all, and equal everywhere—he, that seer, attains my own state, my very nature. 19.
Having shown that saṃsāra is produced by the *guṇas*, [the Lord] shows through two verses that liberation is transcending the *guṇas* and nothing else:
when the living being (*jīva*), as the observer, does not perceive any agent other than the *guṇas* which have transformed into the forms of the agent, the instrument, and the object.
However, he perceives—that is, experiences—that the *guṇas* alone are always the agents.

When he knows the Self as distinct and transcendent from the *guṇas*, then that seer attains—that is, reaches—my state, which is union (*sāyujya*) with me. In this regard, it should be understood through the perspective of the meaning of the concluding verse that even after such knowledge, one must practice supreme devotion toward me. //19//

Baladeva: Having thus described transmigratory existence through the discernment of the *guṇas*, he speaks of liberation through that same discernment in two verses beginning with "not another" (*nānyam*).

When the seer—the individual soul who perceives the true nature of reality—does not perceive any agent other than the *guṇas* which have transformed into the body, senses, and self, but rather perceives the *guṇas* themselves as the agents and knows the Self to be the supreme agent beyond the *guṇas*.
Then he attains My state.
This is the intention: the pure living being (*jīva*), which is consciousness and bliss, is certainly not the performer of actions consisting of suffering such as war and sacrifice;

rather, it is only when associated with a body and senses composed of the *guṇas* that it acts in such a way. Therefore, since it is caused by the *guṇas*, that agency in action resides in the *guṇas* and not in the pure Self—when one perceives this, [one attains My state].
Then, it was previously stated that one attains my state— which is freedom from saṃsāra— or supreme devotion to me; here,
agency caused by the guṇas is denied to the pure [Self].
But it does not culminate in purity;
this has been stated in the passage beginning with "the seer of that" (tasya draṣṭā). //19//
Having transcended these three qualities that arise from the body, the embodied soul, liberated from birth, death, old age, and suffering, attains immortality. 14.20
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says "the qualities" (guṇān) to show that one becomes fulfilled through the cessation of all misfortunes caused by the qualities.
Those whose manifestation and transformation take the form of the body and so forth are "body-born" (deha-samudbhavāḥ).

Having transcended—that is, having gone beyond—these three qualities as well, and being thus liberated from birth and other states produced by them, one attains the immortal, meaning one reaches supreme bliss. //20//
Madhusūdana asks: "How does one attain [this]? It is said: "The qualities (guṇān).
These three qualities—named sattva, rajas, and tamas—which are of the nature of māyā, arise from the body and serve as the seeds for the production of the body.

Having transcended while still living—having sublated [birth, death, etc. through the knowledge of reality—the wise one, being liberated from birth, death, old age, and suffering (including the internal and other types) which consist of illusion, becomes free from connection with them even while alive; thus, as a knower, he attains and enjoys immortality, that is, liberation. //20//
Viśvanātha:
And therefore, he says "the qualities" (guṇān) [in verse 20], meaning that he too is said to have transcended the qualities (guṇātīta).

Baladeva: He clarifies the meaning expressed by the term "my state" with the words "the qualities. Although the embodied soul (jīva) resides within the body, by the power of discriminating between the qualities and the person (puruṣa), it transcends—meaning overcomes—these three qualities arising from the body, which produce the body; thus, liberated from birth and other such conditions, it attains—that is, experiences—the immortal Self.
This state of being Mine, characterized by freedom from saṃsāra, or characterized by being a fit recipient for supreme devotion to Me, is as follows;
thus He will say: "Having become Brahman, with a serene self," and so forth. //20//
By what marks, O Lord, does one become transcendent over these three qualities? What is his conduct, and how does he pass beyond these three qualities? (14.21)

Śrīdhara: Having heard that "one transcends these qualities and partakes of the immortal," Arjuna, desiring to correctly understand the characteristics, the conduct, and the means for transcending the qualities, said: "By what signs, O Lord—by what kinds of marks manifested in the self—does the embodied being become one who has transcended the qualities? This is the question regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
"What is his conduct? means "what is his behavior" (*kim-ācāraḥ*)?
"How does he exist? is the meaning.
And "how," by what means, does he exist having transcended even these three qualities?
"Tell that" is the meaning. //21//
Madhusūdana:

Having heard that "by transcending these qualities, one attains immortality even while living," Arjuna, desiring to properly understand the characteristics, the conduct, and the means for transcending the qualities, said: "By what..."?
"One question is as follows: by what marks is he distinguished who has transcended these qualities? Tell me those marks by which he can be known.
He addresses him as "O Lord" (*prabho*), indicating that, due to his sovereignty, the suffering of his servant must be warded off by the Blessed One himself.
"What is his conduct?"—that is, "What is his mode of behavior? Is he one who acts according to his own whims, or is he one who is restrained? This is the second question.
"Or how, and by what means, does he transcend these three qualities?"—that is, "What is the method for transcending, or going beyond, the qualities? This is the third question. //21//
Viśvanātha:

Although the matter was already asked in the second chapter beginning with "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady," he asks again out of a desire for even greater detail. "By what marks" is one question;
the meaning is: by what signs is that person who has transcended the three qualities (guṇas) to be known?
"What is the conduct? is the second [question].
"And how these [states]? is the third;
the meaning is: what is the means for attaining the state that transcends the qualities (guṇātītatva)?

The distinction is this: whereas previously [in the verse beginning with] "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? it was not asked how one becomes one whose wisdom is steady and who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), that is what is asked now. //21//
Baladeva: With the half-verse beginning with "By what" (*kaiḥ*), Arjuna asks about the characteristics, the conduct, and the means for transcending the qualities (*guṇa*).
The first question means: by what signs can one who has transcended the qualities be known?
The second question, "What is his conduct?", means: is his conduct unrestricted or is it regulated?
"And how these" refers to the third [question]: by what means does one transcend the qualities? This is the meaning. //21//
O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they arise, nor does he long for them when they cease. (14.22)

Śrīdhara: Knowing that the Blessed Lord had already provided an answer in the second chapter— beginning with "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady" (Gītā 2.54)— yet who now asks again out of a desire for further detail, the Blessed Lord spoke in another manner his characteristics and so forth in six verses beginning with "The light" (*prakāśam*).
Therein, he states the characteristic by means of one [verse]: "illumination" (*prakāśam*) refers to the effect of *sattva* previously mentioned as "in all the gates of this body";
and "activity" (*pravṛttim*) is the effect of *rajas*.
And delusion (*moha*) is the effect of darkness (*tamas*);
this is an elliptical expression for [the qualities] beginning with *sattva*.

One who does not feel aversion toward any [of these qualities], even when they have arisen in their respective ways and are spontaneously present, by means of the perception of them as suffering; [that person is a yogin].

And those [qualities] having ceased, he who does not long for them with the notion that they are happiness—he is said to have transcended the qualities; this is the syntactical connection with the fourth verse. //22//
Madhusūdana,

having observed that although the question was already asked in the passage beginning with "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? (Gītā 2.54) and answered in the passage beginning with "When one completely renounces desires" (Gītā 2.55), the seeker asks again from another perspective because he still desires to know more.

The Blessed Lord spoke of its characteristics and so forth by another method in five verses beginning with "prakāśam" (illumination). Listen now to the answer to the question: "By what marks is one who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta) endowed? First, "illumination" refers to all effects.
"Activity" (pravṛtti) is the effect of rajas;
"delusion" (moha) is the effect of tamas.
This is an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa).

All effects of the qualities (*guṇas*), having arisen as they do according to their respective conditions and through the power of their own causal complexes, are of the nature of suffering; yet he who does not hate them with the perception of suffering—likewise, when they cease through the power of the causal complex for destruction, even though they are of the nature of pleasure, he who does not long for or desire them with the perception of pleasure, because he is certain of their falsity like a dream—he who is thus devoid of such hatred and attachment is said to have transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*). This is the syntactical connection following from the fourth verse.
And this definition, which is based on one's own direct perception, is for one's own sake alone, not for the sake of others;
for another is not able to perceive hatred and its absence, or passion and its absence, as they reside within oneself. //22//
Viśvanātha:

Regarding that, he provides the answer to the first question—by what marks does one transcend the qualities (guṇātīta)—stating: "And illumination arises in all the gates of this body"—this is the effect of *sattva*; and "activity," which is the effect of *rajas*.
And delusion is the effect of darkness;
this is an illustration [that includes] the qualities of goodness (sattva) and the rest.
He does not feel aversion toward any of these when they have arisen according to their nature and are spontaneously present, perceiving them as suffering.

The syntactical connection with the fourth verse is as follows: "He who does not long for these effects of the guṇas, even when they have ceased, out of a sense of pleasure—he is said to have transcended the guṇas.
The form *sampravṛttāni* is an archaic neuter plural. (22)

Baladeva: Although this was asked by the verse beginning with "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? and answered by the verse beginning with "When he completely casts off desires," nevertheless, the Lord speaks of his characteristics and so forth in another manner through five verses beginning with "Light... [13.24], because the questioner asks out of a desire for further detail.
Among these, He states the characteristic—which is self-evident—by means of one verse: "Light" is the effect of *sattva*, and "activity" is the effect of *rajas*.

Delusion is the effect of darkness; these three, having proceeded into existence by the power of the causal complex of production, are of the nature of suffering, yet he who does not hate them with the notion that they are suffering;
and having ceased and perished by the power of the causal complex of destruction, they are of the nature of happiness, yet he who does not long for them with the notion that they are happiness.
The connection with the fourth [verse] is as follows: "One who is empty of such hatred and attachment is said to have transcended the qualities.

Since another person is not able to know the presence or absence of hatred and the presence or absence of attachment within oneself, this characteristic is to be personally realized (*svasaṃvedya*). //22//
He who sits as if indifferent, not shaken by the qualities (guṇas), who remains firm thinking "it is only the qualities that are acting," and does not waver— [that person is a sage]. 14.23.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having described the self-evident characteristics of one who has transcended the *guṇas*, he speaks with the three verses beginning with "like one indifferent" (*udāsīnavat*) to provide the answer to the second question—"What is his conduct?"—by describing the characteristics of that person as perceived by others. Being seated like one indifferent, remaining as a witness, he is not shaken from his own nature by the *guṇas*—that is, by the effects of the *guṇas* such as pleasure and pain; rather, it is the *guṇas* themselves that [engage] in their own functions.
They continue to exist; however, one who remains silent through the knowledge of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*), realizing "I have no connection whatsoever with these," [is liberated].
The use of the *parasmaipada* ending is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
It does not stir; it does not move. //23//
Madhusūdana: Thus [the definition of] a *lakṣya*.
Viśvanātha:
He provides the answer to the second question—"What is his conduct?"—with three verses beginning with "udāsīnavat" (like one who is indifferent).

He who is not shaken by the effects of the *guṇas*, such as pleasure and pain—that is, he who does not fall from his state of abiding in his own true nature (*svarūpa*), but rather understands that "it is only the *guṇas* themselves that operate within their respective functions"—remains silent through the knowledge of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*) in the realization that "I have no connection whatsoever with these. [The use of] the *parasmaipada* ending is an archaic Vedic usage; he "does not stir," meaning he does not exert himself in any bodily activity whatsoever.

"He is said to have transcended the qualities"—this means that one should be declared to have transcended the qualities only upon seeing these marks and these conducts; the sense is that one should not be called "transcender of the qualities" merely by being a clever talker who argues for the possibility of transcending the qualities. //23-25//
Baladeva: Now, in order to state the definition of that which is perceivable by another, he provides the answer to the second question—"What is conduct?"—in three verses beginning with "udāsīna.

Just as a neutral person (*udāsīna*), standing in the middle, is not moved from his neutrality by the partisan attachments of two disputants, so too [the Self] is not moved from its established state by the qualities (*guṇas*) such as pleasure and pain, which are colored by those [objects] but do not reside in the Self.
However, having determined that "the qualities (guṇas) abide in their own effects, such as light and so forth,
and I have no connection with them," it remains silent;
it does not move, nor does it act in accordance with the effects of the qualities.
"He is said to have transcended the qualities"—this is the connection with the third [verse]. //23//

He to whom pain and pleasure are equal, who is established in his own self, to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, who is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, who is steadfast, and to whom censure and self-praise are equal; 14.24.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "sameti" means one for whom pleasure and pain are equal;
because he is self-abiding, remaining established in his own true nature.
Therefore, he for whom clods of earth, stones, and gold are equal;
he for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant—which serve as causes for pleasure and pain—are alike; such a person is steadfast and wise.
He for whom self-reproach and self-praise are equal. //24//
Madhusūdana:

He for whom pain and pleasure are equal—by virtue of being devoid of aversion and attachment, by virtue of the selflessness of phenomena (*anātma-dharmatā*), and by virtue of their unreality—is one whose pain and pleasure are equal.
Why is this so? Because he is established in himself, abiding in his own very self (*ātman*) due to being devoid of the perception of duality.
For this very reason, he is one for whom clods of earth, stones, and gold are equal—meaning they are devoid of the status of being either to be rejected or accepted;
"loṣṭa" refers to a lump of dust.

For this same reason, he is one for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant, which are the means to pleasure and pain respectively, are equal, because they are to be regarded with equanimity due to the absence of the cognition that they are means to one's welfare.
He is steadfast, wise, and resolute;

for this very reason, he remains equanimous even toward censure and self-praise—that is, the proclamation of faults and the proclamation of virtues. He who possesses such qualities is said to have transcended the modes; this is the connection with the second verse. //24//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Furthermore, regarding the word "sama" (equal). Since he is established in his own nature (*svastha*), he is one for whom pleasure and pain are equal (*sama-duḥkha-sukha*).
