They are "equal" because they are not properties of the Self; thus, he is one whose pleasure and pain are alike.
He for whom [all things] are equal because they are equally unworthy of being grasped— namely, clods of earth and the like—
is one for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant, the objects that cause pleasure and pain, are equal to a clod of earth or a lump of clay.
He is steadfast (*dhīra*), skilled in the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
The meaning is that for one to whom censure and self-praise are equal, because the defects and virtues that cause them do not reside within himself;
such a person is said to have transcended the qualities—this is the connection with the second [verse]. //24//
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe, and who has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities. 25.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "māna" means:
equal in honor and dishonor;
equal toward the side of friends and the side of enemies.
He whose nature it is to renounce all undertakings and efforts, whether for visible or invisible purposes—one who is endowed with such conduct is said to have transcended the qualities. //25//
Madhusūdana:
*Māna* is honor, synonymous with respect;
*apamāna* is contempt, synonymous with disrespect.
In these two cases, joy and dejection are equally absent.
Censure and praise are of the nature of sound; however, honor and dishonor are specific activities of body and mind that may occur even without sound—this is the distinction.
Here, although there is a variation in the reading between the letters *pa* and *va*, the meaning remains the same.

He is equal toward the factions of friend and enemy; that is, he is not an object of hatred even toward the faction of enemies, or rather, he himself is devoid of both favoring and suppressing them. He has abandoned all undertakings.
"Ārambhāḥ" (undertakings) refers to actions (*karmāṇi*); he whose nature (*śīlam*) is to renounce all of them is "one who has renounced them.
The meaning is that he is one who has abandoned all action except for what is necessary for the maintenance of the body.
He who conducts himself according to the manner described in the verse beginning with "sitting like one indifferent" is said to have transcended the *guṇas*.

The meaning is as follows: that which was stated regarding equanimity and so forth—which must be accomplished through effort prior to the arising of knowledge and is to be practiced as a means by one qualified for knowledge—remains, once knowledge has arisen, as a collection of qualities established without effort as the defining characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) who has transcended the gunas. //25//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: The meaning of "māna" (pride) is clear.
Blame and praise are accomplished through the activity of speech.
The distinction is that honor and dishonor may arise even through the activities of body and mind.
By the word "all," every action other than what is necessary for the mere maintenance of the body is to be understood.

The meaning is that one who is such as this—one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*), whose conduct is as described by the words "like one indifferent" and so forth, and whose behavior is perceived even by others—he is to be known as one who has transcended the qualities; he is not merely a talkative person who speculates about such transcendence. //25//
And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman. 26.
Śrīdhara: [The question is] "How does one transcend these three qualities?
He provides the answer to this question with the words "And me" (māṃ ca).
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

He who serves Me alone, the Supreme Lord, with unswerving and single-minded devotion through the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga), transcends—meaning he completely overcomes—these qualities; he is fit, that is, he becomes capable, for becoming Brahman, which is to say, for liberation. //26//
Madhusūdana says:
"And me" (*māṃ ca*) provides the answer to the third question—how one may now transcend these qualities.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*).

He who serves Me alone— the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller of all beings, who has assumed the state of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through *māyā*, the Blessed Vāsudeva who is a mass of supreme bliss— by means of unswerving *bhakti-yoga* characterized by supreme love as described in the twelfth chapter, and who always meditates upon Me, that devotee of Mine, having completely transcended these aforementioned qualities through the vision of non-duality (*advaita-darśana*), [attains liberation].
Having set aside [all else], it conduces to becoming Brahman—that is, to the state of Brahman, to liberation—and becomes capable [of achieving it];
the meaning is that constant contemplation of the Blessed One alone is the means for transcending the qualities (guṇas). //26//
Viśvanātha:
He provides the answer to the third question—“How does one transcend these three qualities?”—with the words “And me” (māṃ ca).
The word “and” (ca) has the sense of “only” (evārthe).

He who serves Me alone— the Supreme Lord in the form of Śyāmasundara— by means of the yoga of devotion, he indeed attains the state of Brahman, that is, the nature of Brahman or the realization of Brahman; for this is evident from the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in My own statement, "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone" (*bhaktyāham ekayā grāhyaḥ*),
and also from the employment of the particle *eva* in the verse, "Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this Māyā."
This is because of the certainty that the experience of Brahman does not occur through any means other than devotion.
By what kind of yoga of devotion?
By that which is unswerving—that is, unmixed with ritual action, knowledge, and so forth—since the renunciation of desireless action has been taught.
And because it is heard that even knowledge is to be renounced at the final stage of the wise— according to the instruction, "One should renounce [even] knowledge in Me"—
and because no such renunciation of devotional yoga (*bhakti-yoga*) is ever heard of anywhere, that very *bhakti-yoga* alone is unerring.
Therefore, having abandoned both the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) and the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), if one [practices] by means of that unerring [devotion] alone...
If one serves by means of the yoga of devotion, then even a man of knowledge transcends the qualities; it is not otherwise.
For it is stated in the Eleventh [Canto]: "But the devotee who has no other [object of worship], who takes refuge in Me, is indeed beyond the qualities. Thus, he certainly transcends the qualities.

In this regard, the truth is as follows: since it is understood from the verse beginning with "VEṛṣE" that both the ritualist who is free from attachment and the man of knowledge are practitioners by virtue of their very sattvic nature, then—by association with them—it is understood that the devotee, mentioned in the phrase "the one devoid of qualities and taking refuge in Me," is likewise a practitioner. Consequently, the man of knowledge, having become perfected through knowledge, transcends the qualities only after relinquishing his sattvic state.
The meaning obtained is that the devotee (*bhakta*), starting precisely from the stage of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), becomes transcendent of the *guṇas*.
Here, the venerable Svāmī-Caraṇa maintains that the particle "ca" is for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārtha*).
Furthermore, the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī explains: "He who serves Me alone—the Lord Nārāyaṇa—by means of unswerving *bhakti-yoga*, as described in the twelfth and other chapters. //26//
Baladeva: He provides the answer to the third question—“How does one transcend these three qualities?”—with the words “And me” (*māṃ ca*).
The word “and” (*ca*) is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

By the statement beginning with “not another agent apart from the qualities,” it is shown that for one who has attained the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between the qualities and the Puruṣa, the transcendence of the qualities is not accomplished by that [knowledge] alone.

But he who, though possessing those qualities, serves and takes refuge in Me— Kṛṣṇa alone— who am untouched by the modes of *māyā*, the controller of *māyā*, manifested in many ways as Nārāyaṇa and other forms, the mass of consciousness and bliss, the treasure-house of jewels such as omniscience and other divine attributes, through unswerving and exclusive *bhakti-yoga*— he, having transcended and overcome even these difficult-to-cross *guṇas*, attains to the state of Brahman.

It is fit for the attainment of the state distinguished by the eight qualities, meaning it becomes capable of its own inherent nature; the meaning is that it attains that nature. Furthermore, the word "Brahman" applied to the individual soul (jīva) has already been explained previously.
And thus it has been stated that the soul attains its true nature through that discriminative discernment only when it is headed by devotion (*bhakti*), and not by that discernment alone;
as for what was said regarding "attaining the state of Brahman," this refers to my own form.
He explains that "he goes" was taught by the Charioteer of Pārtha; however, that [explanation] is indeed lacking in precision, because even with respect to liberation,

the distinction of essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) has been stated by him in such passages as "by this very knowledge," and so forth, as well as in Vedic texts such as "the stainless one attains the highest equality."

In that regard, because it has been perceived there as being eternal due to its qualities such as atomicity (*aṇutva*) and omnipresence (*vibhutva*), and because its distinction [from Brahman] is eternal,

therefore its state is characterized precisely by the eightfold qualities. As for the two scriptural passages stating "being Brahman, he attains Brahman," the meaning is that being similar to Brahman,
he attains— that is, reaches— Brahman.

This is because the *Viśvaprakāśa* states that "eva" is used in the sense of comparison (*upamya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and the *Amarakośa* states that "vava," "yathā," "tathā," and "eva" are used in the sense of similarity (*sāmya*).
Otherwise, the absorption of Brahmā into the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāvottaro brahmāpyayaḥ*) would not be logically consistent. //26//
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. (14.27)
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this with the words "brahmaṇo hi" (for [I am] of Brahman).
For because I am the support (*pratiṣṭhā*)—that is, the image (*pratimā*)—of Brahman;
I am indeed Brahman itself in its condensed form (*ghanībhūta*).
The meaning is that it is like the solar orb, which is simply light condensed together;
likewise, it belongs to the imperishable and eternal,
because liberation (amṛta) is eternally free.
Likewise, because that means of attainment and the eternal Dharma consist of the nature of the Śiddha-sattva,
and because I am the foundation of absolute and unimpeded bliss,
since my singular form is supreme bliss.
Therefore, since it is inevitable that one who serves Me shall attain My own state, it was rightly said: "he is fit for becoming Brahman."
"In the fourteenth [chapter], it was stated: 'My devotee easily crosses the ocean of worldly existence, which is brought about by attachment to the qualities dependent upon Kṛṣṇa.'"
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division of the Three Guṇas," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana states the reason for this: "of Brahman.

It is the foundation of Brahman—that which is denoted by the term "Brahman," who possesses limiting adjuncts (sopādhika), and who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

The ultimate reality is non-conceptual, consisting of existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), and the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of that word [Brahman].
I am Vāsudeva, the non-conceptual one, who abides "herein"—this "abiding" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the unconstructed form devoid of imagined forms.
Therefore, it is entirely logical that he who serves Me as Brahman with [its] limiting adjuncts is fit for becoming Brahman (*brahmabhūyāya*).
In response to the inquiry, "Of what kind of Brahman am I the foundation?", there are the qualifiers: of the immortal (amṛta), which is devoid of destruction;
of the undecaying (avyaya), which is devoid of transformation;
and of the eternal (śāśvata), which is devoid of diminution.
Of *dharma*, which is characterized by the culmination of knowledge and is to be attained through that *dharma*; and of *sukha*, which is of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

The phrase "of *sukha*" serves to exclude the kind of pleasure born from the contact of sense objects with the senses; rather, it refers to that which is absolute (*aikāntika*), meaning non-deviating (*avyabhicārin*) and existing in all places and at all times, having the form of absolute happiness—this is the meaning.
The meaning is that because I am the true essential nature (*svarūpa*) of such a Brahman, therefore My devotee is liberated from *saṃsāra*.
Thus it was said by Brahmā to the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"You alone are the one Self, the Ancient Person (*puruṣa*)."
"Truthful, self-luminous, infinite, primordial, eternal, imperishable, ever-blissful, stainless,
full, non-dual, liberated from limiting adjuncts, and immortal. [10.14.23] Thus.
In this context, the meaning is that the Self, devoid of all adjuncts (*upādhi*), is Brahman; you are That.
This was also stated by Śuka, even without any formal praise:
"The essential reality of all things remains established as Being."
"O Blessed Kṛṣṇa, what indeed can be described as that which is not this substance? Thus it is said.

For all effect-substances (*kārya-vastu*), the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is their essential nature (*bhāvārtha*), which consists of pure existence (*sattā-rūpa*). This exists within Brahman, which—though appearing in the form of an effect—is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*); for one does not admit an existence of the effect (*kārya-sattā*) that is distinct from the existence of the cause (*kāraṇa-sattā*).

Furthermore, for that very cause—the Brahman with attributes (sopādhika)—the objective reality (bhāvārtha), which is the essence of existence (sattā-rūpa), is Lord Kṛṣṇa; for that which is with attributes is imagined upon that which is without attributes, and what is imagined does not transcend its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). Moreover, because Lord Kṛṣṇa is the substratum of all imagination, he is the nature of the absolute truth (paramārtha-satya), the unconditioned Brahman.

Therefore, what other entity could there be that is not that? What other ultimate reality can be described apart from Śrī Kṛṣṇa? The meaning is that He alone is the sole ultimate reality, and nothing else whatsoever. This very point is stated here as well: "For I am the foundation of Brahman. Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "Granted that Your devotee may attain Your own state, how indeed can he be fit for the state of Brahman, since You are distinct from Brahman? Anticipating this, He says: "For I am the foundation of Brahman."
The meaning is: I alone am the foundation—the ultimate fulfillment—of Brahman, the Supreme Self, and not a Brahman distinct from Me.
Likewise, I alone am the foundation of immortality—that is, of liberation—and of the imperishable, which is never subject to destruction in any way.
The meaning is that liberation culminates in Me alone; liberation is simply the attainment of Me.
Likewise, I alone am the fullness of the eternal Dharma, which has liberation as its fruit and is characterized by steadfastness in knowledge;
the meaning is that the Dharma characterized by steadfastness in knowledge culminates in Me alone, and there is nothing separate from Me to be attained through it.
Similarly, I alone am the fullness of absolute happiness, because My nature is supreme bliss; the meaning is that there is no happiness separate from Me to be attained.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "My devotee is fit for becoming one with Brahman. //27//
I bow to the son of Nanda, the splendorous Supreme Brahman in human form, who has cast aside pride and bondage, and who is the very essence of all beauty.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Division of the Three Guṇas," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
But how can my devotees attain the state of the attributeless Brahman?
That, indeed, could only be possible through the singular experience of that non-dual [reality].
Regarding this, he says: "For [I am] the support of Brahman.
For (*hi*) because Brahman—which is well-known as the supreme support—is itself my support; it is a support (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the sense that "it is supported in this," meaning its substratum.
This is because in all scriptural passages concerning those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, the word "support" (*pratiṣṭhā*) has precisely that meaning.
Likewise, am I not the foundation of immortality?

No; the meaning is that I am the foundation of liberation (*mokṣa*), which is imperishable and free from destruction. Similarly, I am the foundation of the eternal dharma—that supreme dharma called devotion (*bhakti*)—which remains constant even throughout the states of both its practice and its fruition.
Likewise, I am the foundation of the happiness and love associated with the exclusive devotee who attains that [Brahman].
Therefore, because everything is dependent upon Me, one who merges into Brahman through My worship performed with the desire for liberation (kaivalya) also attains the state of Brahman.
Regarding this, the venerable Svāmī-pāda says: "I am the foundation of Brahman; I am indeed Brahman in its condensed form, just as the solar orb is condensed light. This is the meaning.

Just as the sun, although its nature is radiance (*tejas*), is also said to be the substratum (*āśraya*) of that radiance, so too Kṛṣṇa, although His nature is Brahman, is also the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Brahman. On this point, the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* also serves as authority: "He is the auspicious refuge of the all-pervading mind and likewise of the Self" (ViP 6.7.76). Thus, it is established that Kṛṣṇa is both the form of Brahman and the foundation of Brahman. Baladeva: If it be asked, "How can one who has transcended the guṇas, attained his true nature, and is designated as Brahman—that is, the liberated one—remain [in this world] through the discriminative knowledge of that [distinction between self and matter] and through exclusive devotion to You alone?", he says in response: "For of Brahman...
The word "hi" (for) is used for the sake of certainty.

I alone am that very one— the embodiment of consciousness and bliss, possessed of infinite qualities, faultless, the dearest friend, and the Lord of all— released from the cycle of death, immortal, immutable, of a single flavor through that very nature, having manifested my own eightfold qualities upon the transcendence of the veils of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, preceded by that [state] of Brahmā.
I am the beloved of the liberated soul who has emerged from the ocean of death.

According to the Nirukta etymology, "pratiṣṭhā" means that wherein one is established; thus, it refers to Me as the supreme refuge and the most beloved. One who remains while experiencing such a Me with supreme devotion [is called *pratiṣṭhita*].
There is not even a trace of separation from Me, nor does he return again, according to the Smṛtis: "Having gone there, they do not return; that is the supreme goal of the liberated."

If it is asked, "How could one who is already liberated resort to You, since liberation is the fruit of hearing [the scriptures]?"—with the intention that there is indeed a superior fruit, He says: "I alone am the foundation of eternal, common bliss and the nectar of His manifold pastimes.

Thus the Śruti declares: "He is indeed rasa," meaning that one resorts to Me alone for the sake of experiencing His pastimes as a wrestler within the manifestation of that bliss which consists of intense joy.
"For only by obtaining the essence does this [person] become blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1). //27//
Samsara is the conjunction with the gunas, while liberation is the transcendence of the gunas;
that its accomplishment comes through devotion to Hari alone is understood from the fourteenth [chapter].
